claims.text: The initial equiatomic NbMoTaW alloy is single-phase BCC.
The initial NbMoTaW alloy is as-cast.
The initial alloy has a grain size of approximately 50 µm.
Baseline room-temperature tensile ductility is below 5% elongation.
Baseline yield strength at 1600 °C is approximately 600 MPa.
Baseline irradiation swelling is below 1% at 10 dpa.
The proposed intervention adds 0.5 at% B by powder blending, followed by homogenization at 1500 °C for 24 h and hot-isostatic pressing.
Adding approximately 0.5 at% B promotes boron segregation to NbMoTaW grain boundaries.
Boron segregation lowers grain-boundary energy.
Boron segregation increases grain-boundary cohesive strength.
Higher grain-boundary cohesion reduces room-temperature intergranular fracture.
At 0.1–1 at% B, boron remains in solid solution or at grain boundaries rather than forming embrittling precipitates.
Boron addition in the stated range does not create defect sinks that impair high-temperature strength or irradiation tolerance.
B addition increases room-temperature tensile elongation by two to three times relative to baseline.
B addition decreases 1600 °C yield strength by less than 5% relative to baseline.
After irradiation to 10 dpa, swelling remains within 10% of the untreated baseline.
Irradiation creep rate remains within 10% of the untreated baseline.
The modified alloy retains a single-phase BCC structure.
The hypothesis is valid for B contents of 0.1–1 at% and grain sizes of 10–100 µm.
The irradiation-resistance prediction applies at irradiation temperatures no higher than 500 °C.

contradictions.description: The stated baseline is an as-cast alloy, whereas the experiment specifies an undoped control with processing identical to the powder-metallurgy, homogenization, and HIP treatment. These are different baseline states, making the intended comparison ambiguous.

The prediction requires a two- to threefold ductility increase, but falsification occurs only below 10% improvement; an improvement between 10% and twofold would violate the prediction without falsifying the hypothesis.
The predicted 1600 °C strength loss is below 5%, while falsification requires a loss above 10%; a 5–10% loss is inconsistent with the prediction but is not designated as falsifying.
